sections.name: Session 1: Measuring the economy, and money

questions.q: Stagflation describes an economy with:
options: Stable prices together with stagnant wages over several years
High growth together with high inflation, as in an overheating economy
Falling prices together with falling output, as in a depression
Rising prices together with weak growth and rising unemployment
questions.why: Stagnation plus inflation - the mix in which the cure for one problem makes the other worse.

questions.q: A tyre maker sells tyres to a car company, which fits them to new cars. In GDP the tyres are:
options: Counted only if the finished car is exported rather than sold in India
Not counted separately - their value is already inside the price of the car
Counted once, as the car company's investment in equipment
Counted twice - once when sold as tyres and once inside the price of the car
questions.why: They are intermediate goods; counting them again would be double counting.

questions.q: India imports a phone and pays the foreign seller in rupees. What is added to India's GDP?
options: The full price of the phone, because the payment was made in rupees
A reduction equal to the price of the phone, because imports are subtracted
Nothing - the phone was produced abroad, and the currency of payment is irrelevant
Half the price of the phone, shared between the two countries
questions.why: GDP asks where the good was produced. The purchase enters consumption and is removed again as an import.

questions.q: Why are imports subtracted in the GDP identity?
options: Imports displace domestic production, so each rupee imported destroys a rupee of output
C, I and G already include spending on imported goods, which were not produced in the country
The government taxes imports, and taxes are not part of production
Imports are paid for in dollars, which have to be removed from a rupee total
questions.why: Subtracting imports only removes foreign production that entered through C, I and G.

questions.q: A sweet maker produces extra stock in September for Diwali, and it is still unsold when the quarter ends. In that quarter's GDP the stock is:
options: Counted twice - now and again when sold
Counted as inventory investment
Left out until it is sold
Counted as consumption
questions.why: Unsold output is treated as bought by the firm itself. When it sells, inventories fall and consumption rises.

questions.q: A forestry company sells logs for 1,000 to a furniture maker, who sells furniture for 2,500 to a retailer, who sells it to a consumer for 3,000. The contribution to GDP is:
questions.why: GDP is the value of the final good: 3,000, which equals 1,000 + 1,500 + 500 of value added.

questions.q: An economy produces 5 apples in both years, and the price rises from Rs. 20 to Rs. 40. Then:
options: Nominal GDP is unchanged and real GDP doubles
Both are unchanged
Nominal GDP doubles and real GDP is unchanged
Nominal and real GDP both double
questions.why: Nominal GDP goes from 100 to 200 on price alone; at base-year prices output is still 100.

questions.q: A firm's sales grew 9% in a year in which its prices rose 5%. Its volume growth was about:
questions.why: Rupee growth is roughly price growth plus volume growth, so 9 - 5 = 4.

questions.q: The CPI is 114.3 in 2004 and 117.1 in 2005. Inflation in 2005 is:
questions.why: (117.1 - 114.3) / 114.3 = 2.5%. Subtracting the two index numbers gives 2.8, which is the common mistake.

questions.q: Inflation falls from 8.1% to 2.5%. This means that prices are:
options: Falling
Unchanged
Back at their base-year level
Still rising, but more slowly
questions.why: Lower inflation is a slower rise. Prices fall only when inflation is negative.

questions.q: Engel's law states that:
options: The poor spend a smaller share of income on food than the rich
As income rises, the share of income spent on food falls
Food prices rise faster than incomes
As income rises, spending on food falls in rupees
questions.why: The share falls even though the rupee amount usually rises.

questions.q: Core inflation is:
options: Wholesale price inflation
Inflation in food and fuel only
Inflation in services only
Headline inflation with food and fuel taken out
questions.why: Core strips out the two most volatile groups to show the underlying trend.

questions.q: A one-year loan carries a nominal rate of 4% and inflation is expected to be 6%. The real interest rate is:
questions.why: 4 - 6 = -2%. The lender gets back less purchasing power than he lent.

questions.q: A borrows Rs. 10,000 from B at 5% while inflation runs at 10%. Who gains?
options: B, because he earns 5% interest on money that would otherwise lie idle
A, because he repays in rupees that buy less; B's real return is about -5%
Both, because the loan allowed A to spend and B to earn
Neither, because the interest received exactly offsets the inflation
questions.why: Unexpected inflation favours the borrower.

questions.q: Money is defined as:
options: The stock of assets that can be readily used to make transactions
The gold and foreign currency held by the central bank
The income a person earns over a year from all sources
The total wealth a person owns, including house and shares
questions.why: Income is a flow, and most wealth - a house, say - cannot be used to pay a bill.

questions.q: Seigniorage is:
options: The central bank's profit: interest earned on its assets, none paid on currency
The fee the government pays the central bank to have currency notes printed
The interest the government pays to all the holders of its bonds
A tax collected from commercial banks on the deposits that they hold
questions.why: Liabilities at 0%, assets earning interest: the difference is seigniorage.

questions.q: Quantitative easing (QE) is best described as:
options: Raising the policy interest rate in large, pre-announced steps to fight inflation
Cutting the cash reserve ratio to its legal minimum in a single, pre-announced step
A large, pre-announced government spending programme funded by fresh borrowing
Large, pre-announced bond purchases by the central bank when the policy rate is near its floor
questions.why: When the price lever is stuck near zero, the central bank works through quantity.

questions.q: The government sells Rs. 10,000 crore of new bonds to banks and mutual funds. As a result:
options: The RBI's balance sheet expands by Rs. 10,000 crore
Rs. 10,000 crore of new money is created, because bonds are a form of money
The money supply rises by the multiplier times Rs. 10,000 crore
Existing money moves from the buyers to the government; no new money is created
questions.why: Money is created only when the central bank buys bonds with new reserves.

questions.q: The correct order of transmission after a repo-rate cut is:
options: Borrowing rises, then loan rates fall, then banks' cost of funds falls, then money shrinks
Banks' cost of funds falls, loan rates fall, borrowing rises, and more loans create more money
Deposits rise, then banks' cost of funds falls, then the RBI cuts, then loan rates fall
Loan rates fall, then banks' cost of funds falls, then borrowing rises, then the RBI cuts
questions.why: The chain runs from the RBI to banks to borrowers, with a lag at each step.

questions.q: In the classroom cascade with R = 10%, the third bank receives a deposit of Rs. 81. It keeps and lends:
options: Rs. 8 and Rs. 73
Rs. 9 and Rs. 81
questions.why: 10% of 81 is 8.10; the remaining 72.90 is lent. Rs. 7.29 and Rs. 65.61 is what the fourth bank does.

questions.q: The actual multiplier is far below 1 / CRR mainly because:
options: The effective CRR is far higher than the announced 3%
The RBI limits bank lending to a fixed multiple of capital each year
People hold part of their money as cash, and banks do not lend all they are allowed to
Deposits created by loans are not counted in the money supply
questions.why: These are the two points of the critique on the slides: cash leakage and banks holding back.

questions.q: Maturity mismatch in a bank means:
options: Short-term deposits are funding long-term loans
Its lending and deposit rates differ
Long-term deposits are funding short-term loans
Its assets and liabilities are in different currencies
questions.why: Banks borrow short and lend long - it is what banking is.

questions.q: A bank has deposits of 1,000, reserves of 100 and sound loans of 900. Depositors demand 300 in one day. The bank:
options: Is closed automatically by the RBI, because its reserves are below 30% of deposits
Recalls enough of its loans from borrowers the same afternoon to pay everyone
Cannot pay from its reserves and may fail, because good loans cannot quickly be turned into cash
Pays easily, because sound loans can be counted as cash when depositors ask
questions.why: A solvent bank can still be illiquid.

questions.q: Deposit insurance in India covers each depositor up to:
options: Rs. 1 lakh per bank
An unlimited amount
Rs. 5 lakh per bank
Rs. 50 lakh per bank
questions.why: Above that limit, money in a bank is an unsecured claim on the bank.

questions.q: Suppose real GDP growth is 7.8%, CPI inflation is 4.82% and the repo rate is 5.25%. Which statement is true?
options: The real policy rate is mildly positive, and inflation is above target but inside the band
Nominal growth must be below real growth, because inflation is positive
The real policy rate is negative, because inflation is close to the repo rate
Inflation is below the 4% target, so the RBI has room to cut
questions.why: 5.25 - 4.82 is about +0.4%, and 4.82% lies between 4% and 6%.

questions.q: A CRR of 3% implies a textbook multiplier of about 33, yet India's actual multiplier is about 6. The best explanation is that:
options: The textbook formula was designed only for developed economies
The RBI holds back a large part of the base money that it creates each year
People hold cash, and banks do not lend every rupee they are allowed to
Banks are in practice required to keep reserves of about 16% of deposits
questions.why: Cash in wallets stops multiplying, and lending depends on banks' and borrowers' willingness. 1/R is only a ceiling.

questions.q: Which of the following works on B rather than on m?
options: Households moving their savings from cash into deposits
Commercial banks becoming more willing to extend loans
A cut in the cash reserve ratio announced by the RBI
The RBI buying government bonds with newly created reserves
questions.why: An open market purchase adds to base money itself. The other three change how far a given base is multiplied.

questions.q: In terms of M = m x B, India's experience in 2020 is best described as:
options: Both B and m rose strongly at the same time
B and m were both unchanged through the year
B rose but m fell, offsetting much of the rise
B fell while m rose, leaving M unchanged
questions.why: The RBI expanded the base; banks did not lend it on, so the multiplier adjusted downwards.

questions.q: An issuer has 50 billion dollars of coins outstanding, fully backed by Treasury bills yielding 4%. Its annual interest income is about:
options: 200 million dollars
4 billion dollars
2 billion dollars
12.5 billion dollars
questions.why: 50 billion x 4% = 2 billion a year, none of which is passed to coin holders.

questions.q: Under the GENIUS Act, interest paid by a stablecoin issuer to holders of its coin is:
options: Left to each state to decide
Prohibited
Allowed, but capped at 2% a year
Compulsory, at the Treasury bill rate
questions.why: Issuers are barred from paying holders interest or yield - one of the things that separates the coin from a deposit.

questions.q: If nominal GDP grows 10.3% and real GDP grows 7.8%, the prices of domestically produced output rose by about:
questions.why: Nominal growth is roughly real growth plus price rise: 10.3 minus 7.8 is about 2.5.

questions.q: Double deflation means:
options: Deflating output and intermediate inputs separately, then subtracting
Using two different base years, one for goods and one for services
Deflating GDP by the CPI and by the WPI, and averaging the two
Removing the effect of inflation twice from the same figure
questions.why: Real value added = real output minus real inputs, each valued at its own base-year prices.

questions.q: Actual GDP is 104 and potential GDP is 100. The economy has:
options: A positive output gap of 4% and is overheating
A recession, since output differs from potential
A negative output gap of 4% and idle capacity
A budget surplus equal to 4% of its GDP
questions.why: Output above capacity is a positive gap - the overheating case, with pressure on wages and prices.

questions.q: A country invests 100 this year while 30 of its existing capital wears out. Its capital stock changes by:
options: Plus 100
Minus 30
Plus 130
Plus 70
questions.why: Net addition = investment minus depreciation = 100 - 30 = 70.

questions.q: Firms decide whether to hire one more worker by looking at:
options: Their total output
The marginal product of labour
Last year's profit
The average product of labour
questions.why: Every decision of a firm is taken at the margin: what will the next person add?

questions.q: A branch clears 400 cheques a day with 8 clerks. After computerisation 2 clerks clear all 400. The average product per clerk has moved from:
options: 8 to 2
questions.why: 400 / 8 = 50 before; 400 / 2 = 200 after. Average productivity has quadrupled.

questions.q: In the water-bottle economy there is ONE bottle, and citizens' money is doubled from Rs. 100 to Rs. 200 each. The outcome is:
options: Price Rs. 100, one bottle sold
Price Rs. 200, two bottles sold
Price Rs. 200, one bottle sold
Price Rs. 100, two bottles sold
questions.why: Capacity is one bottle, so the extra money can only bid up the price.

questions.q: Using M = P x Y with output fixed at one bottle, raising money from 100 to 300 gives a price of:
questions.why: P = M / Y = 300 / 1. With output fixed, the price level moves one for one with money.

questions.q: Deflation is:
options: A fall in real GDP for two successive quarters
A sustained fall in the general level of prices
A fall in the rate of inflation, say from 6% to 3%
A fall in the exchange value of the currency
questions.why: A falling inflation rate is disinflation - prices still rise. Deflation is prices themselves falling.

questions.q: The Pigou effect failed in the Great Depression mainly because:
options: Falling prices led people to expect further falls, so they waited
The money supply was expanding very rapidly at the time
Governments were running very large budget deficits
Prices did not in fact fall during those years, so the mechanism was never tested
questions.why: Deflation creates deflationary expectations - the piece Pigou's argument left out.

questions.q: The paradox of thrift says that when everyone tries to save more:
options: Total income falls, so total saving may not rise at all
The government's deficit falls by the same amount
Investment rises automatically to absorb the saving
Interest rates rise and bring spending back
questions.why: If all cut spending together, all incomes fall, and nobody ends up safer.

questions.q: Your salary rises 6% in a year in which prices rise 8%. Your real wage has:
options: Fallen by about 2%
Risen by 6%
Fallen by 8%
Risen by about 2%
questions.why: Real wage change is roughly pay rise minus inflation: 6 - 8 = -2.

questions.q: If T = 90 and G = 110, the budget shows:
options: Public saving of 20, held in reserve
A balanced position, since both are near 100
A deficit of 20, financed by issuing bonds
A surplus of 20, which is public saving
questions.why: G - T = 20. The gap is borrowed by selling government bonds.

questions.q: By the test given in class, government spending is "productive" if it:
options: Is spent on salaries rather than on purchases of goods
Is financed out of taxes rather than out of borrowing
Is disbursed quickly after the budget is passed, so that it reaches people without delay
Increases the economy's capacity to produce in the future
questions.why: If capacity rises, there are more goods tomorrow for the money to chase, so the spending need not be inflationary.

questions.q: With an MPC of 0.8, the Keynesian multiplier is:
A tax cut of Rs. 100 has a smaller multiplier than Rs. 100 of government spending because:
options: Government spending is never saved or taxed away
Part of the tax cut is saved before any of it is spent
Tax cuts are not permitted during a recession
Tax cuts push up interest rates more than spending does
questions.why: All 100 of spending enters round one; of a tax cut only the 80 that is spent does. Hence 4 rather than 5.

questions.q: The money supply doubles while the price level is unchanged. On the diagram this is shown as:
options: A shift of the AD curve to the right
A movement up along the AD curve
A movement down along the AD curve
A shift of the AD curve to the left
questions.why: At the same price more is demanded - the whole curve moves. Only a change in P itself is a movement along it.

questions.q: A stablecoin issuer, a commercial bank and a money market fund all take money from the public. Which of them multiplies deposits by lending to firms and households?
options: None of the three
Only the stablecoin issuer
The issuer and the fund
Only the commercial bank
questions.why: Only the bank lends on what it receives, and so only the bank creates money.

sections.name: Session 3: Supply, expectations and the open economy

questions.q: In the COVID years the combination of policies in most countries was:
options: Contractionary fiscal policy with contractionary monetary policy
Expansionary fiscal policy with contractionary monetary policy
Contractionary fiscal policy with expansionary monetary policy
Expansionary fiscal policy with expansionary monetary policy
questions.why: Governments spent more than they taxed, and central banks bought the bonds with new money.

questions.q: With an expansionary budget but a tightening central bank, which business is most likely to struggle?
options: A grocery retailer selling daily essentials
A seller of cars bought mostly on loans
A chain of neighbourhood pharmacies
A maker of toothpaste and soap sold for cash
questions.why: Incomes are supported by the budget, but credit is costly - so goods bought on borrowed money suffer most.

questions.q: A stock-market boom makes households feel richer and spend more, though their salaries are unchanged. This is:
options: The Keynesian multiplier at work on consumer spending
The crowding out of private spending by the state
The wealth effect - a rise in autonomous consumption
The Pigou effect produced by a falling price level
questions.why: Wealth, not income, has changed. Demand shifts right with no policy action at all.

questions.q: The Keynesian short-run supply curve is horizontal because:
options: Output is fixed by the economy's stock of capital and labour
Wages are perfectly flexible and adjust every week
The money supply is held constant by the central bank
Prices are stuck, so firms meet changes in demand by changing output
questions.why: In the short run it is output, not price, that responds - depending on how much capacity firms use.

questions.q: A unit costs Rs. 5 to make and sells for Rs. 6. The price rises to Rs. 7 while the cost stays at Rs. 5. Profit per unit:
options: Is unchanged at Re 1
Trebles, from Re 1 to Rs. 3
Doubles, from Re 1 to Rs. 2
Rises by one half
questions.why: 6 - 5 = 1 before; 7 - 5 = 2 after. Each extra unit now earns twice as much.

questions.q: If producers correctly realise that ALL prices have risen in the same proportion, they will:
options: Leave output unchanged, since nothing real has changed
Close down until prices return to normal
Cut their own prices to gain market share
Produce a great deal more than before, to profit from the higher prices
questions.why: Their price relative to their costs is the same as before, so there is no reason to produce more.

questions.q: On the class slide the economy moves from A (output 7,500, unemployment 7%, inflation 2%) to B (output 8,000). At B:
options: Unemployment is 10% and inflation is 2%
Unemployment is 4% and inflation is 2%
Unemployment is 7% and inflation is 6%
Unemployment is 4% and inflation is 6%
questions.why: More output, so fewer unemployed; higher prices, so more inflation.

questions.q: In the Phillips curve equation, inflation rises above expected inflation when:
options: Unemployment is equal to its natural rate
Unemployment is below its natural rate
The natural rate itself is rising
Unemployment is above its natural rate
questions.why: A labour market tighter than normal pushes wages, and therefore prices, up faster than people expected.

questions.q: On the class slide, extra money first takes the economy from output 10 and inflation 2% to output 11 and inflation 3.5%. After expectations have adjusted, it ends at:
options: Output 10, inflation 5.5%
Output 11, inflation 5.5%
Output 10, inflation 2%
Output 11, inflation 3.5%
questions.why: Output returns to potential; the only lasting effect of the extra money is higher inflation.

questions.q: A rate hike differs from quantitative tightening in that a rate hike:
options: Works only by reducing the government's spending
Removes money from the system directly, by selling bonds
Has no effect of any kind on the supply of money
Raises the price of money, reducing its quantity only indirectly
questions.why: QT works on the quantity directly. A rate hike works on the price and cuts the quantity through less lending.

questions.q: The wage-price spiral is a loop in which:
options: Higher wages lower prices by raising productivity
Prices rise while wages are held down by long contracts
Higher prices raise expected inflation, then wages, then costs, then prices again
Wages and prices fall together, year after year, as firms and workers undercut one another in turn
questions.why: Each turn feeds the next, so inflation no longer needs an outside cause.

questions.q: "Inflation should be low enough that nobody talks about it" means that price stability is achieved when:
options: The prices of goods and services stop changing altogether
The rate of inflation equals the rate of economic growth
Wages are frozen by agreement between firms and workers
Inflation does not enter the decisions of households and firms
questions.why: Once people talk about prices, they build inflation into their wage demands and plans.

questions.q: A negative supply shock moves inflation and output in which directions?
options: Inflation up, output down
Inflation up, output up
Inflation down, output up
Inflation down, output down
questions.why: A demand shock moves both the same way; a supply shock gives the worst of both.

questions.q: The central bank faces this dilemma after a supply shock because:
options: Supply shocks are always permanent
Its instrument acts on demand and cannot move supply
The government's budget is too tight to help
It has run out of foreign exchange reserves
questions.why: Money shifts the demand curve. It cannot produce oil or rain.

questions.q: Inflation falling from 8% to 4% is ________; inflation moving from 4% to minus 4% is ________.
options: Disinflation; disinflation
Deflation; disinflation
Disinflation; deflation
Deflation; deflation
questions.why: In the first case prices are still rising; in the second they are actually falling.

questions.q: The "sacrifice ratio" measures:
options: The ratio of government debt to GDP
The output or employment lost for each point taken off inflation
The ratio of a country's exports to its imports of goods and services
The share of national income that is saved
questions.why: It is the price of disinflation. Senator Kennedy's 3.6 points of unemployment for 2 points of inflation is one estimate.

questions.q: Senator Kennedy's rule from history was 3.6 points of unemployment for every 2 points taken off inflation. With inflation at 6.4% and unemployment at 3.4%, reaching 2.4% inflation would need unemployment of:
questions.why: Four points off inflation is twice 3.6, or 7.2 points more unemployment: 3.4 + 7.2 = 10.6.

questions.q: The index suggests that fragmentation today is:
options: About the same as it was in the year 2000
Higher than it was during the 1970s
At the lowest level in the whole series
Lower than it was during the 1970s
questions.why: It has climbed since 2008 to the highest level in the series.

questions.q: The open-economy identity derived in class is:
options: S - I = M - X
S - I = X - M
S = X - M
S + I = X + M
questions.why: Saving minus investment equals exports minus imports.

questions.q: India exports 100 and imports 150. Foreign investors bring in 100. The country's foreign exchange reserves:
options: Fall by 50
Rise by 50
Rise by 100
Are unchanged
questions.why: 50 of the inflow pays for the trade gap; the RBI buys the other 50.

questions.q: The rate moves from Rs. 90 to Rs. 92 per dollar. Then:
options: Both currencies have depreciated
The rupee has appreciated and the dollar has depreciated
The rupee has depreciated and the dollar has appreciated
Both currencies have appreciated
questions.why: More rupees are needed for the same dollar: the dollar is dearer, the rupee cheaper.

questions.q: A foreign tourist visiting the Taj Mahal is, in the country's external accounts:
options: A remittance from abroad
An import of goods into India, since the visitor consumes what is produced here
An inflow of foreign capital
An export of services, raising the demand for rupees
questions.why: The visitor buys Indian services - hotel, transport - and needs rupees to do it.

questions.q: A car costs Rs. 71 lakh in India - about 86,600 dollars at Rs. 82 - and a similar car costs 105,900 dollars in the US. The real exchange rate, the American car in terms of Indian cars, is about:
questions.why: 105,900 / 86,600 = 1.22. The reverse, 0.82, is one Indian car in terms of American cars.

questions.q: In the class exercise the buyer's demand is Q = 87 - 0.082 x P, with P in dollars. XYZ raises its price to Rs. 90,000 while the rate is Rs. 84, so the dollar price is about 1,071. Units demanded are:
options: Zero
questions.why: 87 - 0.082 x 1,071 is negative: at that price the buyer takes nothing.

questions.q: The United States raises interest rates. The most likely effect on India is that:
options: Capital floods into India in search of safety, and the rupee strengthens
India's exports to the United States stop
Capital is drawn toward dollar assets and the rupee tends to weaken
India's saving rises above its investment
questions.why: Higher US rates raise the demand for dollar assets; foreign saving is slower to arrive in India.

sections.name: Session 4: Exchange rates and the world outside

questions.q: The exchange rate moves from 5 Malaysian ringgit per dollar to 4 ringgit per dollar. Then:
options: Both currencies have depreciated
The dollar has depreciated and the ringgit has appreciated
The dollar has appreciated and the ringgit has depreciated
Neither currency has changed in value
questions.why: A dollar now buys fewer ringgit, so the dollar is weaker and the ringgit stronger - the example on the slide.

questions.q: A car is invoiced in rupees. Its price doubles from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 1,00,000 while the rupee moves from Rs. 50 to Rs. 80 per dollar. The American buyer, who used to pay 1,000 dollars, now pays:
options: 1,000 dollars
625 dollars
2,000 dollars
1,250 dollars
questions.why: 1,00,000 / 80 = 1,250 dollars - more than the original 1,000, although the rupee has fallen.

questions.q: "The adjustment happens on the revenue side rather than the demand side" describes:
options: Rupee invoicing: the buyer's price changes and so does the quantity sold
Dollar invoicing: quantity is unchanged and the exporter's rupee revenue changes
A devaluation announced by the government
A fixed exchange rate defended by the central bank
questions.why: With the dollar price fixed, demand does not respond; the exporter's home-currency income does.

questions.q: According to the class, the choice of invoicing currency depends mainly on:
options: The size of the customer's national economy
The tax laws of the seller's home country
The payment technology available to the buyer
How much pricing power the seller holds
questions.why: "It is a function of how much monopolistic power you hold. Who will bear the risk?"

questions.q: Under dollar currency pricing, who bears the exchange-rate risk in the short run?
options: Nobody, because the dollar price is fixed
The importer, whose local-currency cost moves with the exchange rate
The central bank of the importing country
The exporter, whose home-currency revenue changes with the rate
questions.why: The dollar price is fixed for a time, so the buyer's cost in its own currency rises and falls with the rate.

questions.q: When the RBI sells dollars and takes in rupees, India's money supply:
options: Doubles
Is unchanged
Falls
Rises
questions.why: The rupees it receives are withdrawn from circulation.

questions.q: The "impossible trinity" says that a country cannot have all three of:
options: A fixed exchange rate, free movement of capital and its own monetary policy
A budget surplus, low rates of taxation and a high level of public spending
High exports, low imports and rising reserves
Low inflation, low unemployment and high growth
questions.why: It can choose any two of the three, never all three.

questions.q: The correct pairing of regime and vocabulary is:
options: Both regimes - devaluation and revaluation
Fixed rate - depreciation and appreciation; flexible rate - devaluation and revaluation
Fixed rate - devaluation and revaluation; flexible rate - depreciation and appreciation
Both regimes - depreciation and appreciation
questions.why: Governments devalue; markets depreciate.

questions.q: On 6 June 1966 India:
options: Devalued the rupee by 36.5%, from Rs. 4.76 to Rs. 7.50 per dollar
Allowed the rupee to float freely
Nationalised its largest commercial banks
Became a member of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank
questions.why: The front page shown in class: "Rupee devalued by 36.5 per cent."

questions.q: Governor Malhotra's statement of November 2025 was that the RBI:
options: Had devalued the rupee to help exporters
Would stop intervening in the currency market
Does not target any level for the rupee; the depreciation was driven by dollar demand
Would defend the rupee at Rs. 85 to the dollar for as long as its reserves allowed it to do so
questions.why: Not a fixed regime: no line it has promised to hold.

questions.q: In the week to 18 September 2026 India's reserves fell by almost 15 billion dollars. This indicates that the RBI had been:
options: Buying dollars to stop the rupee rising
Revaluing its holdings of gold upward
Lending dollars to the government
Selling dollars to steady the rupee
questions.why: Oil was dearer and the Fed had just raised rates; the rupee was allowed to weaken, but not to slide.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four spillovers the RBI listed in 2022?
options: A fall in the prices of imports
Capital outflows
Pressure on the currency to depreciate
Loss of reserves
questions.why: The fourth was imported inflation - imports became dearer, not cheaper.

questions.q: India is exposed to the Fed's decisions because, by the identity S - I = X - M, it:
options: Keeps its exchange rate fixed against the dollar at all times
Saves less than it invests, and relies on foreign saving
Exports more than it imports
Saves more than it invests
questions.why: Anything that makes foreign saving prefer to stay at home is felt here at once.

questions.q: "Import cover" measures:
options: Imports as a percentage of GDP
How many months of imports the reserves could pay for
The insurance carried on imported shipments
The tariffs charged on a country's imports of goods and services
questions.why: It makes countries of different sizes comparable.

questions.q: Import cover fell from about 17 months in 2021 to about 10-11 months although reserves in dollars are near a record, because:
options: The RBI stopped counting gold in the reserves
The dollar lost value against the rupee
Imports have grown, so the same reserves cover fewer months
Gold in the reserves lost most of its value during those years
questions.why: The measure is reserves divided by monthly imports; the denominator has risen.

questions.q: The professor's argument against large-scale de-dollarisation was that:
options: The dollar is backed by the gold held by the US government, which no other currency can match
The International Monetary Fund does not permit it
If the world were abandoning the dollar, demand for it could not be weakening other currencies
The euro has failed as an international currency
questions.why: Both statements cannot be true in any large way.

questions.q: Transaction exposure is the risk that:
options: The exchange rate changes the home-currency value of a payment agreed but not yet made
The accounts of a foreign subsidiary change in value when they are consolidated with the parent's
A firm's competitive position is eroded over several years
The interest rate on a loan rises before it is repaid
questions.why: A deal already struck, not yet settled.

questions.q: An exporter is due 1,00,000 dollars in 90 days and sells them forward at Rs. 96. If the rate on the day is Rs. 92, it receives:
options: Rs. 98 lakh
Rs. 96 lakh
Rs. 94 lakh
Rs. 92 lakh
questions.why: The forward rate applies whatever the market rate turns out to be.

questions.q: The same exporter instead buys an option to sell at Rs. 95, paying a premium of Re 1 per dollar. If the rate turns out to be Rs. 98, it nets:
options: Rs. 95 lakh
Rs. 94 lakh
Rs. 98 lakh
Rs. 97 lakh
questions.why: It lets the option lapse and sells at 98; less the premium of Rs. 1 lakh, that is Rs. 97 lakh.

questions.q: The Plaza Accord of 1985 was an agreement among five countries to:
options: Act together to bring down the value of the dollar
Create a common European currency
Fix their exchange rates permanently against one another
Raise the price of oil
questions.why: The United States, Japan, West Germany, France and the United Kingdom.

questions.q: According to S - I = X - M, a tariff by itself:
options: Changes what is imported and from whom, not the saving-investment gap that sets the deficit
Eliminates the trade deficit within a year, provided that other countries do not retaliate at all
Raises the country's saving rate
Lowers investment by the amount of the tariff
questions.why: The deficit lasts as long as saving falls short of investment.

questions.q: The proposal to charge foreign holders of US Treasury debt a fee "needs co-operation from the Fed" because:
options: The Fed must approve every trade agreement
The Fed would be the agency responsible for collecting the fee from foreign governments
If foreigners sell bonds and long-term rates rise, the Fed may have to buy the bonds
The Fed is responsible for setting tariffs
questions.why: Buying government bonds with new money to hold rates down - the very thing central-bank independence is meant to prevent.

questions.q: "Focus on innovation" follows from this session's lesson that:
options: The rupee floats freely
Only pricing power lets a firm pass currency risk to its customers
Tariffs are always temporary, so a firm need only wait for them to be removed
India's reserves are at a record
questions.why: A product others cannot copy is what lets you invoice on your own terms.

questions.q: The Fed raises rates; India's reserves fall by 15 billion dollars in a week while the rupee weakens modestly. This is consistent with:
options: A free float with no intervention
A managed float in which the RBI sold dollars to slow the fall
A fixed rate that was successfully defended by the central bank
A devaluation of the rupee
questions.why: Under a peg the rupee would not have moved; under a free float the reserves would not have. AFTER THE FOUR SESSIONS

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three reasons given in class for a manager to study macroeconomics?
options: To analyse the contemporary economic condition
To forecast the firm's own share price for the next quarter
To comprehend the words and signals of policymakers and factor them into decisions
To analyse the boundary conditions within which a business operates
questions.why: The three reasons are boundary conditions, the current condition and policymakers' signals; share-price forecasting was never on the list.

questions.q: In the formula M = m x B, the letter B stands for:
options: Bank deposits held by households and firms across the banking system
The monetary base: currency plus banks' reserves with the central bank
Broad money, including the time deposits that the public holds with banks
The government bonds held as assets on the central bank's balance sheet
questions.why: B is base (reserve) money - the layer the central bank creates directly. Deposits belong to M, the second layer.

questions.q: The quarrel between President Trump and Fed chair Powell was at root a case of:
options: Both policies turning expansionary at the same time
Both policies turning contractionary at the same time
Contractionary fiscal policy meeting expansionary monetary policy
Expansionary fiscal policy meeting contractionary monetary policy
questions.why: A tax cut pushed demand up while the Fed raised rates and shrank its bond holdings to hold demand down.

questions.q: A country whose saving is greater than its investment is:
options: A net borrower from the rest of the world, with a trade deficit
A net lender to the rest of the world, with a trade deficit
A net borrower from the rest of the world, with a trade surplus
A net lender to the rest of the world, with a trade surplus
questions.why: S greater than I means X greater than IM. Lenders run surpluses; borrowers run deficits.

questions.q: A Korean company runs a phone factory in Noida. The output of that factory is part of:
options: Both countries' GDP in full
Neither country's GDP
India's GDP
Korea's GDP only
questions.why: GDP follows geography, not ownership. It was produced on Indian soil.

questions.q: A 10% reserve ratio turns Rs. 100 into Rs. 1,000 of deposits; a 90% ratio turns it into Rs. 111. The reason is that a lower ratio:
options: Makes the RBI issue fresh currency notes at every round of lending
Increases the amount of base money that exists in the banking system as a whole
Lets more of each deposit be lent on, so the chain runs for more rounds
Raises the interest rate that banks have to pay depositors to attract funds
questions.why: The base is unchanged at 100. Less is locked up per round, so more rounds of lending and depositing take place.

questions.q: "Autonomous" consumption or investment means spending that:
options: Changes without any change in income or in policy
Rises only when household incomes have risen first
Is financed directly out of the government's budget
Is undertaken by autonomous public-sector bodies
questions.why: It comes from optimism or from wealth - people or firms deciding to spend more of their own accord.

questions.q: After a real depreciation of the rupee, India's:
options: Exports and imports both fall by the same amount
Exports rise and imports fall, so net exports rise
Exports fall and imports rise, so net exports fall
Exports rise and imports rise by the same amount
questions.why: Buyers at home and abroad switch towards the relatively cheaper Indian goods.

questions.q: You sell a ten-year-old flat for Rs. 80 lakh through a broker who charges Rs. 80,000. The addition to this year's GDP is:
options: Zero
Rs. 80 lakh
Rs. 80.8 lakh
questions.why: The flat was produced years ago; only the broker's service was produced this year.

questions.q: When the RBI cut the cash reserve ratio from 4% to 3% in 2025, what changed?
options: The monetary base rose; the multiplier did not change at all
Both the monetary base and the multiplier rose together
Neither changed; a CRR cut only moves the repo rate
The ceiling on the multiplier rose; the monetary base did not change
questions.why: A CRR cut creates no new base money. It lets banks lend more of each deposit - it works on m, not on B.

questions.q: The classical view that "supply creates its own demand" implies that the aggregate supply curve is:
options: Upward sloping: output rises as the price level rises
Horizontal: prices are fixed and output adjusts to demand
Downward sloping: output falls as the price level rises
Vertical: output is fixed by capital, labour and technology
questions.why: If prices adjust freely, everything produced is sold, and output depends only on the economy's capacity.

questions.q: Under a dollar invoice fixed at 1,000 dollars, when the rupee moves from 50 to 80 the buyer pays:
options: 1,600 dollars
1,250 dollars
1,000 dollars, as before
625 dollars, as in Case 1
questions.why: The buyer's price is set in dollars, so the exchange rate does not touch it.

questions.q: A team in Bengaluru monitors a customer's factory in Texas remotely and bills the customer in dollars. The service is counted in:
options: US GDP, because it is used there
Both countries' GDP in full
Neither, because nothing physical crosses a border
India's GDP, as an export of services
questions.why: It is produced in India; where it is consumed decides only that it is an export.

questions.q: Banks were reluctant to lend in 2020 for all of the following reasons EXCEPT:
options: Fear of later investigation if a loan went bad
Bad loans carried over from the previous decade
Few safe borrowers in a locked-down economy
A ban on fresh lending imposed by the RBI
questions.why: There was no ban - the RBI and the government wanted banks to lend. The reluctance was the banks' own.

questions.q: In the Keynesian short run, what decides how much firms produce?
options: The size of the capital stock and nothing else
The price level that firms expect next year
The natural rate of unemployment in the economy
The level of demand at the prices already set
questions.why: With prices fixed, firms produce whatever is demanded, using more or less of their capacity.

questions.q: A car is invoiced at 1,000 dollars. When the rupee moves from Rs. 50 to Rs. 80 per dollar, the exporter's rupee receipts per car:
options: Stay at Rs. 50,000
Rise from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 62,500
Rise from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 80,000
Fall from Rs. 80,000 to Rs. 50,000
questions.why: 1,000 dollars converts into 80,000 rupees at the new rate.

questions.q: A household buys a newly built apartment from the builder. In the national accounts this is:
options: Investment (I) - residential
Government purchases (G)
Consumption (C)
Not counted
questions.why: New housing is investment, the one large item of I that households rather than firms buy.

questions.q: "He was paying interest on his own money" refers to:
options: The government paying interest to the RBI on the bonds the RBI had bought
Small firms paying interest on loans that the government had guaranteed
Banks paying interest to their depositors on balances they could not lend
The RBI paying banks interest on money it had created and they had parked back
questions.why: The RBI created the money, banks deposited it back through the reverse repo, and the RBI paid them interest on it.

questions.q: The sticky-wage model explains the upward-sloping supply curve by saying that when prices rise:
options: Firms are misled about what is happening to the price level
The central bank expands money to match the higher prices
Wages rise faster than prices, so workers supply more labour
Wages lag behind, so profit per unit rises and firms produce more
questions.why: Prices are slow to change but wages are slower; the gap between the two is extra profit on every unit.

questions.q: An AI subscription is priced in dollars for Indian customers. When the rupee falls:
options: The company receives fewer dollars; the customer pays the same rupees
Both the company and the customer lose equally
The customer pays more rupees; the company's dollar revenue is unchanged
Neither the company nor the customer is affected
questions.why: With a dollar price the risk sits with the customer - the professor's own rising bill.

questions.q: A farmer sells wheat to a miller for $1; the miller sells flour to a baker for $3; the baker sells bread for $6. The miller's value added is:
questions.why: 3 - 1 = 2. The three value-added figures (1, 2, 3) sum to the $6 price of the bread.

questions.q: The government's most direct answer in 2020 to banks' fear of lending to small firms was to:
options: Guarantee the loans, so the risk of default did not fall on the bank
Close the reverse repo window so that banks could not park cash
Order the RBI to lend to small firms from its own balance sheet
Have the repo rate cut to zero until the lockdowns were lifted
questions.why: "Give the loan, I am the guarantor" - credit-guarantee schemes for MSMEs removed the banker's fear directly.

questions.q: In Lucas's imperfect-information model a producer raises output when her price rises because she:
options: Believes her price has risen relative to other prices
Finds that wages have fallen in her industry
Receives a subsidy linked to the price she charges
Expects the price of her product to fall soon
questions.why: She reads a general rise in prices as a rise in demand for her own product.

questions.q: A streaming service that sells in a crowded market prices in rupees for its Indian customers because:
options: Its market is competitive: customers would leave if their bill rose whenever the rupee fell
Indian law requires every subscription sold to consumers in India to be priced and billed in rupees
UPI cannot be used to pay a price that is set in dollars
All of its costs are incurred in rupees
questions.why: With several rivals a click away, it cannot make customers carry the currency risk.

questions.q: In April-June 2026 India's nominal GDP grew 10.3% and real GDP grew 7.8%. The difference mainly reflects:
options: The growth of imports
A statistical discrepancy
Population growth
The rise in prices
questions.why: The gap between nominal and real growth is the price change, measured by the GDP deflator.

questions.q: Money held in a UPI app is:
options: A central bank digital currency issued directly to users by the RBI
Tokenised but not digital, since it is recorded on a public blockchain
Digital but not tokenised: it is still entries in banks' own ledgers
A stablecoin that is issued and guaranteed by the payments network
questions.why: UPI moves entries between banks' private books. A tokenised rupee would itself live on a shared ledger.

questions.q: The natural rate of unemployment is the rate that prevails when:
options: Inflation has fallen to zero
No one is between jobs or searching for work
The government's budget is in balance
Output is equal to potential output
questions.why: Even at potential some unemployment remains - frictional and structural.

questions.q: Which measure of inflation does the RBI target?
options: Core CPI inflation
WPI inflation
The GDP deflator
Headline CPI inflation
questions.why: The target is headline CPI, although the RBI watches core closely.

questions.q: Because so much trade is invoiced in dollars, a fall in the rupee reaches the Indian economy first as:
options: An immediate surge in the volume of goods and services exported
A fall in the rate of inflation
Costlier imports, with export volumes responding slowly
Lower prices for imported goods
questions.why: Dollar-priced exports are no cheaper for foreign buyers; dollar-priced imports cost more rupees at once.

questions.q: The institution a stablecoin issuer most closely resembles, according to the class, is a:
options: Commercial bank
Stock exchange
Central bank
Money market fund
questions.why: Like a money market fund it pools the public's cash into Treasury bills and repos; unlike the fund, it keeps the interest.

questions.q: India's large number of young people who are not trained for the jobs on offer is an example of:
options: Cyclical unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
Structural unemployment
questions.why: The people and the jobs both exist; the skills do not match. More demand alone will not fix it.

questions.q: In a fixed exchange-rate system the central bank:
options: Lets the market decide the rate each day
Changes the announced rate every day, in line with the demand and supply it observes
Takes no part in the currency market
Stands ready to buy and sell foreign currency at the announced rate
questions.why: Because it will always deal at the fixed price, nobody deals at any other.

questions.q: The GDP deflator differs from the CPI because the deflator:
options: Includes imported consumer goods such as phones and fuel
Covers only the goods and services that households consume
Covers everything produced domestically, including capital goods and government services
Uses a basket of items that stays fixed until the base year changes
questions.why: The first three describe the CPI or are simply wrong for the deflator.

questions.q: "Dollarisation", the risk that central banks outside the US fear from stablecoins, means:
options: Banks from emerging economies opening branches and taking deposits inside the United States
Households and firms moving savings and payments into dollars, weakening the home currency
The US government buying up the currencies of emerging economies in the foreign exchange market
A sustained fall in the value of the dollar against the currencies of emerging economies
questions.why: If people save and pay in dollar tokens, the home central bank's tools reach less and less of the economy.

questions.q: After a rise in the money supply, what carries the economy from the short-run result (more output) to the long-run result (only more inflation)?
options: A rise in the economy's potential output
The adjustment of expected prices, which shifts aggregate supply
A cut in taxes by the government
A fall in the money supply back to its original level, engineered by the central bank
questions.why: People revise their expectations and ask for higher wages; costs rise and the supply curve shifts up.

questions.q: India's present exchange-rate system is best described as:
options: A fixed rate
A free float with no intervention
A managed float
A currency board
questions.why: The market sets the rate; the RBI steps in from time to time to steady it.

questions.q: A sharp rise in the price of imported smartphones will show up in:
options: The GDP deflator but not the CPI
Both equally
Neither
The CPI but not the GDP deflator
questions.why: Households buy them, so CPI rises; they are not produced in India, so the deflator does not.

questions.q: Some critics compared Rs. 88.27 lakh crore on the new GDP series with Rs. 86 lakh crore on the old one and called it 2.6% growth. That figure is wrong because it:
options: Compares a new-series number with an old-series number
Uses real numbers where nominal numbers are needed
Ignores the growth of population between the two years
Leaves the informal sector out of the calculation
questions.why: 88.27 (new method) against 86.05 (old method) mixes two rulers. The professor said it makes no economic sense.

questions.q: On 16 September 2026 the US Federal Reserve:
options: Raised its policy rate by 25 basis points, to 3.75-4.00%
Cut its policy rate by 25 basis points
Raised its policy rate by 100 basis points
Left its policy rate unchanged for a sixth meeting
questions.why: From 3.50-3.75% to 3.75-4.00%, with a signal that more could follow.

questions.q: "The interest rate becomes endogenous" under a fixed exchange rate means that:
options: The interest rate is fixed for ever at its present level
The interest rate is decided by the government in its budget instead of by the central bank
The central bank can no longer choose it; it is dictated by the need to hold the rate
The interest rate falls to zero and stays there
questions.why: Holding the exchange rate decides the money supply, and so the interest rate.

questions.q: Between the 2012 and 2024 baskets, the all-India combined weight of food and beverages moved from about:
questions.why: 54.2 to 44.8 is the rural figure and 36.3 to 34.3 the urban one.

questions.q: A higher policy rate reduces the money supply indirectly because:
options: The government prints fewer currency notes that year
Savers withdraw their deposits and hold cash instead
Costlier loans mean fewer loans, so the deposit-loan chain creates less money
Banks are then required to hold a larger part of their deposits as gold in their own vaults
questions.why: Money is created when banks lend. Fewer loans mean fewer rounds of the multiplier.

questions.q: Households can feel inflation near 5% while the GDP deflator shows about 2.5% because the CPI, unlike the deflator:
options: Leaves out food and fuel, whose prices are the most volatile
Is compiled only once a year and so lags behind actual prices
Covers machinery, construction and government services as well
Tracks the household shopping basket, including imported goods
questions.why: The deflator covers everything made in India and excludes imports; the CPI covers what households buy, wherever made.

questions.q: A country wants a fixed exchange rate AND an interest rate of its own choosing. By the impossible trinity it must:
options: Restrict the movement of capital across its borders
Let its currency float freely against all other currencies
Hold no foreign exchange reserves
Give up having a central bank
questions.why: With capital unable to leave, a different interest rate does not drain the reserves.

questions.q: Headline inflation is high only because of vegetable prices, while core inflation is low. A rate hike:
options: Will bring vegetable prices down quickly by cooling the demand for food
Cannot grow more vegetables, so the RBI may look through a temporary supply shock
Is compulsory under the law whenever headline inflation is above 4%
Will raise core inflation by making loans to food traders costlier
questions.why: Interest rates act on demand. A supply shock in food is not cured by costlier loans.

questions.q: A firm makes the same quantity of goods from the same quantity of inputs as last year. Output prices are flat and input prices fall 10%. Its real value added has:
options: Risen by 10%
Fallen by 10%
Not changed
Risen by the saving on inputs
questions.why: Nothing real changed - only the margin in rupees. Single deflation would wrongly report growth; double deflation reports zero.

questions.q: If inflation expectations rise, workers demand higher wages. For firms this acts like:
options: A negative supply shock: costs rise and the supply curve shifts left
A positive supply shock: costs fall and output rises
A fall in the money supply engineered by the central bank
A positive demand shock: sales rise at every price, and the demand curve shifts right
questions.why: A rise in wages is a rise in costs, whatever caused it.

questions.q: Saying that "the rupee was devalued today" is wrong for the present-day rupee because:
options: The rupee never loses value against the dollar for more than a few days, so the word cannot apply
Only the RBI is permitted to use the word
The rupee's rate is set by the market, so it depreciates; devaluation belongs to a fixed rate
The word has been dropped from economics
questions.why: The professor was blunt about writers who mix the two.

questions.q: According to the Fisher equation, the real interest rate is approximately:
options: The nominal rate multiplied by expected inflation
The nominal rate minus expected inflation
The nominal rate plus expected inflation
Expected inflation minus the nominal rate
questions.why: i = r + expected inflation, so r = i - expected inflation.

questions.q: The professor used popular songs about rising prices as evidence that:
options: People are talking about inflation - a sign that expectations are not anchored
Official inflation figures are exaggerated, since songs are written about only a few goods
The consumer price index is wrongly constructed
Real wages are rising across the country
questions.why: "The economy is people, not aliens." What people talk about is what they act on.

questions.q: Which combination is typical of a negative output gap?
options: The central bank raising interest rates
Labour shortages and fast-rising wages
Prices rising faster than the target
Idle capacity and rising unemployment
questions.why: Below potential, machines and people are idle. The other three belong to an overheating economy.

questions.q: India's second devaluation, in July 1991, took the rupee from about:
options: Rs. 21 to Rs. 26 per dollar
Rs. 8 to Rs. 12 per dollar
Rs. 45 to Rs. 60 per dollar
Rs. 4.76 to Rs. 7.50 per dollar
questions.why: Reserves had fallen to a few weeks of imports; the fixed rate was abandoned within two years.

questions.q: A fixed deposit pays 7%. Interest is taxed at 30% and inflation is 5%. The real after-tax return is about:
options: Just below zero
questions.why: After tax the deposit earns 4.9%; against 5% inflation that is about -0.1%.

questions.q: The "Golden Rule" level of saving (called the golden ratio in class) is the saving rate that:
options: Gives the highest consumption the country can sustain in the long run
Brings the government's budget exactly into balance each year
Produces the largest stock of capital that the economy could possibly accumulate
Matches the investment rate of the fastest-growing large economy
questions.why: Too little saving means too little capital; too much means giving up consumption for nothing.

questions.q: After a negative supply shock, a central bank that expands money in order to restore output will:
options: Leave inflation where it was
Shift the supply curve back to where it began
Bring inflation down at the same time
Push inflation higher still
questions.why: Protecting output: output recovers, at the cost of even more inflation.

questions.q: A rise in world demand for India's software services, other things equal:
options: Weakens the rupee, because more dollars are needed to pay for them
Reduces India's foreign exchange reserves
Raises the demand for rupees and limits the rupee's depreciation
Has no effect on the exchange rate
questions.why: Companies and individuals move the rate in the same way the RBI does - through demand and supply.

questions.q: Unexpected inflation transfers wealth from:
options: Exporters to importers
Borrowers to lenders
The government to households
Lenders and savers to borrowers
questions.why: Debts are repaid in cheaper money. The biggest borrower, the government, is the biggest gainer.

questions.q: Which of these would raise India's potential GDP?
options: A faster rise in the supply of money and bank credit
A rebate on personal income tax for salaried households
A technology that lets the same workers and machines produce more
A cut of half a percentage point in the repo rate by the RBI's rate-setting committee
questions.why: The first three move demand. Only capital, labour and technology move capacity.

questions.q: The RBI Governor whose term (2008 to 2013) was marked by costly oil, weak monsoons and inflation near 10% was:
options: D. Subbarao
Shaktikanta Das
Raghuram Rajan
Urjit Patel
questions.why: Rajan succeeded him in September 2013 and began the disinflation.

questions.q: Restrictions on imports, or on taking money abroad, manage the exchange rate by:
options: Reducing the demand for dollars
Creating more rupees
Increasing the supply of dollars
Raising interest rates
questions.why: They are the capital-control corner of the impossible trinity.

questions.q: Fiat money has value because:
options: It is backed one-for-one by gold
It is costly to print
It has intrinsic value as paper
Everyone expects everyone else to accept it
questions.why: Its value is a shared belief, reinforced by the state accepting it for taxes.

questions.q: According to the class, the early unemployment caused by a new technology is eventually reversed mainly when:
options: Wages fall far enough to make hiring attractive again
The central bank cuts interest rates to support demand
The government restricts the use of the technology
The technology creates new tasks for which people are needed
questions.why: Computers removed the ledger clerk and created ATMs, cards, net banking and analytics. New tasks restore hiring.

questions.q: A central bank can sometimes "look through" a supply shock when the shock is:
options: Expected to last for many years
Temporary, and expectations remain anchored
Caused by excessive demand in the economy
Larger than five percentage points
questions.why: One bad monsoon reverses itself. The danger is only that it raises expectations and so becomes permanent.

questions.q: "Imported inflation" arises when:
options: Wages at home rise faster than the productivity of the workers who earn them
A country's exports grow faster than its imports
The central bank expands the money supply
The currency falls, so goods bought abroad cost more in home currency
questions.why: Oil at the same dollar price costs more rupees when the rupee is weaker.

questions.q: On the three-function test, Bitcoin's clearest weakness today is that:
options: It cannot be transferred between people without going through a bank
It cannot be divided into units small enough for everyday payments
Prices and salaries are not quoted in it, and its value swings too sharply
It is illegal to hold or trade in every major economy of the world
questions.why: It fails as a unit of account and as a stable store of value, and is rarely used as a medium of exchange.

questions.q: One explanation for why AI is a louder worry in India than in the US was that in the US:
options: The labour market is tight and new tasks are being created fast
Companies have been much slower to adopt AI tools
Wages are set by the government and cannot be cut
Labour law prevents firms from laying off their workers
questions.why: America is running above potential, with more demand for workers than supply, and is quick to build new tasks.

questions.q: In the first stage of a disinflation the central bank:
options: Shifts aggregate supply to the right by lowering firms' costs
Reduces aggregate demand, pushing output below potential
Cuts taxes in order to support household incomes
Raises potential GDP by encouraging investment
questions.why: It raises interest rates; demand shifts left; output and inflation both fall. This is the pain.

questions.q: A rise in the Fed's interest rate is, for the United States and for India respectively:
options: A tax on American consumers; a subsidy to Indian exporters that raises their dollar prices
A devaluation of the dollar; a revaluation of the rupee
A way of cooling demand; a rise in the return on dollar assets that pulls capital away
A fiscal stimulus; a fiscal contraction
questions.why: Session 3 saw it from America's side; this session sees it from the other end.

questions.q: On the RBI's balance sheet, a currency note in your pocket is:
options: A liability
An asset
Not recorded at all
Part of its capital
questions.why: The note is the RBI's promise to pay the bearer - a debt it owes.

questions.q: In the version of the water-bottle economy with a full warehouse and a price tag fixed at Rs. 100, doubling everyone's money leads to:
options: Price Rs. 200, one bottle sold
Price Rs. 200, two bottles sold
Price Rs. 100, two bottles sold
Price Rs. 50, two bottles sold
questions.why: With a sticky price and spare capacity, the quantity adjusts instead of the price.

questions.q: Powell's phrase "a sustained period of below-trend growth" means:
options: Output growing faster than its potential for a time
A period in which the budget is balanced
A period in which inflation is exactly zero
Output deliberately held below potential for a time
questions.why: A central banker's way of saying that a slowdown is intended.

questions.q: According to the "painless disinflation" argument, inflation can fall without higher unemployment if:
options: Wages and prices are frozen by law for a year
The government raises its spending at the same time
The central bank's commitment is credible, so expected inflation falls at once
The central bank acts quietly, without announcing its intentions to the public in advance
questions.why: If people believe the announcement, expectations fall first and inflation can follow without a slump.

questions.q: The three "prices" of money are:
options: The CPI, the WPI and the GDP deflator
The repo rate, the cash reserve ratio and the statutory liquidity ratio
Wages, rent and profit - the three kinds of income
The interest rate, the price level and the exchange rate
questions.why: Money priced against time, against goods, and against other currencies.

questions.q: "Involution", as the word was used in class, describes:
options: A wave of mergers and takeovers that steadily reduces the number of competitors in an industry
Firms cutting prices to gain share, forcing rivals to follow, until all margins shrink
A government setting minimum prices for every firm in an industry
Exporters turning back to the home market when foreign demand falls
questions.why: A price war nobody wins: no one gains share for long, everyone's margin is thinner, and wages follow.

questions.q: One cost of holding very large reserves is that:
options: They are held in safe foreign assets that pay little
They earn a higher return than any other asset
They cannot be used in a crisis
They push up the price of imports
questions.why: Reserves are insurance, and insurance has a premium.

questions.q: A fall of several billion dollars in reserves within a week most likely signals that:
options: Inflation in India has fallen below target
The RBI has been selling dollars; the rupee was under pressure
The RBI has been buying dollars from the market
Exports have risen sharply during the week, bringing in more dollars
questions.why: The rupee wanted to fall further than it did.

questions.q: A repo-rate hike and QT are:
options: Both forms of tightening, one through the price of money and the other through its quantity
Both fiscal measures, taken by the government rather than the central bank
Opposite in effect - a rate hike tightens while QT eases
The same thing under two names - both reduce the quantity of money directly
questions.why: They are different levers that push in the same direction.

questions.q: During deflation, a borrower paying a fixed EMI finds that the real burden of the loan:
options: Disappears
Rises
Stays the same
Falls
questions.why: The EMI is fixed in rupees while prices and salaries fall, so it takes a larger share of income.

questions.q: Senator Kennedy's central argument to Powell was that:
options: If Congress slowed spending and borrowing, the Fed could put fewer people out of work
Unemployment is of no importance when inflation is high
Interest rates should be cut at once to protect jobs, whatever the effect on prices might be
The Fed should give up trying to reduce inflation
questions.why: Demand can be reduced from the fiscal side as well as the monetary side; sharing the load shortens the pain.

questions.q: Dollar invoicing supports the dollar's dominance because:
options: Other currencies cannot legally be used for trade
The World Trade Organization requires it
Even trade that never touches the United States needs dollars
The United States is a party to most of the world's trade
questions.why: Oil and most commodities are priced in dollars, whoever buys and sells them.

questions.q: The RBI buying bonds directly from the government at the time of issue would be:
options: The same as a repo, because the bonds are later bought back
Something the law requires at the end of every quarter
Monetisation of the deficit - the automatic version ended in April 1997
A routine open market operation of the kind carried out every week
questions.why: The RBI buys in the secondary market; a direct purchase is printing money to fund spending.

questions.q: The central Keynesian claim is that:
options: Governments should balance their budgets in every single year, whatever the state of the economy
Money has no effect on output or employment at any horizon, short or long
Inflation is always and everywhere the result of rising wages
Markets do not correct themselves, so government must act to restore demand
questions.why: Keynes was the first to say it plainly, and it gave governments a far larger role in the economy.

questions.q: What actually happened in the months after the Kennedy-Powell hearing of March 2023?
options: Unemployment rose above 10%, very much as the historical rule had predicted
Inflation fell to about 3% while unemployment stayed under 4%
Inflation climbed back above 9%
The United States entered a deep recession
questions.why: History had predicted far more pain than came.

questions.q: Translation exposure arises when:
options: A rival's currency falls sharply
An export invoice has not yet been paid and the exchange rate moves in the meantime
The results of foreign subsidiaries are converted into the parent's currency
Tariffs are changed without notice
questions.why: It is an effect on the financial statements.

questions.q: According to the index, the long fall in fragmentation - the era of globalisation - ran roughly from:
options: The early 1990s to 2008
The end of the war in 1945 to 1975
questions.why: Before it, the Cold War years were high and steady; after it, fragmentation rose.

questions.q: When rural demand weakened after COVID, the first response of Indian FMCG companies, as, was to:
options: Withdraw from the smaller rural markets
Cut prices on all their main products
Raise prices in order to protect margins
Keep the price point and reduce the pack size
questions.why: Sticky prices in action: the Rs. 5 and Rs. 10 points stayed and the grams came down.

questions.q: The interest rate on a Rs. 50 lakh, 20-year home loan falls from 9% to 8%. The monthly EMI falls by about:
questions.why: From about Rs. 44,990 to about Rs. 41,820 - which is why EMI-driven demand follows the repo rate.

questions.q: A natural hedge is:
options: Entering a forward contract with a bank
Matching the currency of costs or borrowing to the currency of revenue
Insurance against currency losses that is bought from a government agency
Buying a currency option from a bank
questions.why: A fall in the rupee then raises costs and revenue together.

questions.q: In a fractional reserve banking system, banks:
options: Lend only their owners' capital and leave deposits untouched
Keep all deposits as reserves and earn a fee for safekeeping
Pass all deposits to the central bank, which does the lending
Keep a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest
questions.why: Because depositors do not all withdraw at once, a fraction is enough on a normal day.

questions.q: "Government never pays. You pay" makes the point that:
options: The central bank finances whatever the government spends
Governments in practice never repay what they borrow
Companies, not individuals, bear the whole tax burden
Public spending is ultimately financed by taxpayers, now or later
questions.why: A government has no income of its own beyond taxes and, at the edges, the proceeds of its assets.

questions.q: Joseph Stiglitz's prediction, recalled in class, was that the decade after the financial crisis would be one of:
options: Falling inequality within rich countries
Faster globalisation than ever before
Stronger international institutions
Populist leaders, as after the Great Depression
questions.why: Hardship leaves people asking what globalisation has done for them; the anger builds into politics over years.

questions.q: A forward at Rs. 96 that "loses" because the rate ends at Rs. 98 has:
options: Cost the firm part of its capital
Broken the firm's hedging policy
Done its job: it replaced an unknown outcome with a known one
Failed, and shows that forward contracts should not be used again
questions.why: Hedging is not a way to make money. Judge it by whether the business could plan.

questions.q: "A fractional reserve banking system creates money, but not wealth" because:
options: The borrower's new cash is matched by a new debt of the same size
Banks keep the interest, so the gain goes to them and not to society
The RBI takes back the new money through the reserve requirement
Inflation immediately wipes out the value of the new money
questions.why: Spending power rises; net worth does not.

questions.q: Germany's past budget surpluses were described in class as a way of:
options: Forcing the economy to save more, making capital cheap for investment
Reducing the volume of the country's exports to its European neighbours
Lowering saving in order to boost household consumption
Paying for a more generous system of welfare benefits
questions.why: Tax more than you spend and the state saves on the citizens' behalf - cheap capital, more factories, more exports.

questions.q: A country that exports more than it imports must be:
options: Investing more than it saves
Consuming more than it produces
Running a deficit in its government budget
Saving more than it invests
questions.why: If X - M is positive, S - I must be positive. There is no third possibility.

questions.q: The US administration presents its tariffs as:
options: A form of quantitative easing
A subsidy paid to American exporters
A source of revenue for the government, with no effect on trade or the currency
A tool for correcting an overvalued dollar and a wide trade deficit
questions.why: "Tariffs as currency tools" - one more form of intervention.

questions.q: According to the identity, a country's trade deficit can shrink only if:
options: It changes the currency in which it invoices
The gap between its saving and its investment narrows
It imposes a tariff on its largest trading partner
It changes the list of goods that it imports
questions.why: Tariffs change what is imported and from whom; the total is set by saving and investment.

questions.q: The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is:
options: The ratio of a household's saving to its investment
The share of income that is paid in taxes
The share of total income that a household consumes
The part of an extra rupee of income that is spent
questions.why: It is about the extra rupee - the margin - not the average share of income consumed.

questions.q: "Loans create deposits" means that:
options: Deposits are, in effect, loans made by the public to the RBI
Loans are paid out in cash, which borrowers then deposit elsewhere
A bank must first collect a deposit of equal size before it can make each loan
When a bank grants a loan it credits the borrower's account, creating a new deposit
questions.why: The bank finds the reserves afterwards, at around the repo rate.

questions.q: A tariff on imported inputs acts on the home economy like:
options: A positive supply shock: costs fall and output rises
A fall in the money supply
A negative supply shock: costs and prices rise
A fiscal stimulus
questions.why: Session 3: anything that raises the cost of production shifts supply left.

questions.q: A bank run is:
options: A bank expanding its lending faster than its capital allows
A sudden rush by investors to buy a bank's shares
A sharp, unexpected rise in interest rates announced by the RBI
Many depositors withdrawing at once because they fear the bank will fail
questions.why: The fear can be self-fulfilling, even when the bank is sound.

questions.q: With an MPC of 0.75, government spending of Rs. 200 crore raises total income by:
options: Rs. 267 crore
Rs. 150 crore
Rs. 1,000 crore
Rs. 800 crore
questions.why: The multiplier is 1 / 0.25 = 4, and 4 x 200 = 800.

questions.q: If Indian interest rates rise relative to those abroad, the rupee tends to:
options: Depreciate, because money becomes scarce at home
Appreciate, because foreigners buy more Indian bonds and need rupees
Depreciate, because exports become dearer
Stay unchanged, because interest rates are a domestic matter
questions.why: Higher returns raise the demand for Indian assets, and so for rupees.

questions.q: A weaker dollar would be helped by lower US interest rates because:
options: Dollar assets then pay less, reducing the demand for dollars
Lower interest rates raise American saving
Lower interest rates automatically raise the tariffs charged on imports
Lower interest rates fix the exchange rate
questions.why: The chain of Section 4.08, run in reverse.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a defence against bank runs?
options: Reserve and liquidity requirements
Paying higher dividends to shareholders
The central bank acting as lender of last resort
Deposit insurance
questions.why: Dividends take money out of the bank; the other three build confidence or cushions.

questions.q: CRISIL said the effect of the GST cuts would depend on pass-through and on whether consumption rose. "Pass-through" refers to:
options: How soon tax refunds reach the companies
How quickly the new rates were notified and came into force across the states
Whether the states share the loss of revenue
Whether companies lower prices by the amount of the tax cut
questions.why: Gate 1: only if prices actually fall is it as though the consumer's income had risen.

questions.q: A car costs Rs. 71 lakh in India and a similar car costs 105,900 dollars in the US. At Rs. 82 per dollar the Indian car costs about:
options: 105,900 dollars
58,200 dollars
86,600 dollars
71,000 dollars

questions.q: The "user fee" recommendation attributed to Stephen Miran would be charged on:
options: American exporters
American households
American commercial banks and pension funds
Foreign holders of US Treasury debt
questions.why: The dollar is strong because the world wants to hold US government bonds.

questions.q: A company funds a ten-year plant with ninety-day borrowings that must be renewed every quarter. The risk it is running is the same as:
options: Seigniorage
Engel's law
Stagflation
A bank's maturity mismatch
questions.why: Long assets on short money - one bad quarter in the credit market can be fatal.

questions.q: Compared with a GST cut, an income-tax cut:
options: Depends on companies reducing their prices
Puts money directly in taxpayers' hands, so only the MPC matters
Benefits only the buyers of imported goods
Has no effect at all on consumer demand, because income tax is paid only once a year
questions.why: There is no company in between deciding whether to pass it on - only the second gate remains.

questions.q: The formula given in class is: real exchange rate =
options: Nominal exchange rate - inflation abroad
Nominal exchange rate x (price at home / price abroad)
Nominal exchange rate x (price abroad / price at home)
Nominal exchange rate + inflation at home
questions.why: 82 x 105,900 / 71,00,000 = 1.22. A rise in this number is a real depreciation of the rupee.

questions.q: Offshore operations act as a hedge because:
options: They remove currency risk completely
They always reduce the wage bill
They spread costs and revenues across more than one currency and jurisdiction
They allow a firm to avoid paying taxes in any of the countries where it operates
questions.why: A natural hedge built into where the firm operates.

questions.q: The revenue of an Indian IT services exporter sits in which component of India's GDP?
options: NX
I
C
G
questions.why: Services sold abroad are exports. [Session 1]

questions.q: A fall in the general price level, with nothing else changed, causes:
options: A movement along the AD curve to a higher quantity demanded
No change at all in the quantity demanded
A shift of the whole AD curve to the right, as after a rise in the money supply
A shift of the whole AD curve to the left
questions.why: A change in P moves you along the curve. Shifts come from money, spending, taxes or confidence.

questions.q: In the class exercise the real exchange rate began at 1.50. With the rate at Rs. 84 and XYZ's price raised to Rs. 90,000 it becomes 84 x 1,500 / 90,000, which is:
options: 0.71 - a real depreciation of the rupee
1.50 - no change in real terms
1.40 - a real appreciation of the rupee from 1.50
1.54 - a real depreciation of the rupee from 1.50
questions.why: Indian goods have become dearer relative to American ones although the rupee fell in nominal terms.

questions.q: The rupee falls 10% and an exporter's rupee costs also rise 10%. Billing in dollars, its position is:
options: Better, since it will sell more units
Much better, since it now earns more rupees on every dollar that it bills abroad
Much worse, since its costs have risen
Unchanged in real terms: more rupees per dollar, offset by higher costs
questions.why: A depreciation helps the exporter only so long as costs at home have not risen to match it. [Session 4]

questions.q: Which statement about money creation is correct?
options: The RBI creates all money; commercial banks only pass it on to borrowers
The RBI creates base money; commercial banks create most of broad money by lending
The government creates money when it spends; the RBI only records it
Commercial banks create base money; the RBI creates deposits
questions.why: Two layers: reserves and currency from the RBI, deposits from banks. [Session 1]

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches each multiplier with its "leak"?
options: Money multiplier - saving; Keynesian multiplier - reserves
Money multiplier - reserves; Keynesian multiplier - saving
Money multiplier - taxes; Keynesian multiplier - depreciation
Money multiplier - depreciation; Keynesian multiplier - taxes
questions.why: Banks hold back reserves at each round; households hold back saving. [Session 2]

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes a successful disinflation?
options: Demand shifts left; expectations fall; supply shifts right; output returns to potential
Demand shifts right; expectations rise; supply shifts left; output returns to potential at higher inflation
Supply shifts left, then demand shifts right
Demand shifts right, then supply shifts right
questions.why: Short pain while output is below potential; the gain arrives when expectations and supply adjust. [Session 3]

questions.q: A country with a fixed rate, free capital flows and falling reserves faces a rise in US interest rates. The likely sequence is:
options: Its currency appreciates and its reserves rise
Its interest rates fall, its exports boom and its reserves rise within a few months
It sells reserves, its interest rates rise, and if reserves run low it devalues
Nothing changes, because the rate is fixed
questions.why: Sections 4.05 and 4.06 in order. [Session 4] THE LAST FEW PAGES
